claim: PRRS was discovered in the United States in 1987.
source: Since its discovery in the United States in 1987, PRRS has rapidly spread worldwide, with frequent outbreaks causing large economic losses (Holtkamp et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holtkamp et al., 2013

claim: PRRS has rapidly spread worldwide with frequent outbreaks causing large economic losses.
source: Since its discovery in the United States in 1987, PRRS has rapidly spread worldwide, with frequent outbreaks causing large economic losses (Holtkamp et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holtkamp et al., 2013

claim: Three surface receptors on porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs) function in PRRSV invasion in vivo: heparin sulphate (HS), sialoadhesin (Sn), and CD163.
source: Three surface receptors on porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs) have been shown to function in PRRSV invasion in vivo: heparin sulphate (HS), sialoadhesin (Sn), and CD163 (Calvert et al., 2007; Crocker and Gordon, 1986; Jusa et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calvert et al., 2007; Crocker and Gordon, 1986; Jusa et al., 1997

claim: CD163 is an essential receptor for PRRSV infection.
source: Multiple studies have reported that CD163 is an essential receptor for PRRSV infection, with scavenger receptor cysteine-rich domain 5 (SRCR5) serving as the core domain for virus recognition (Calvert et al., 2007; Van Gorp et al., 2010; Patton et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calvert et al., 2007; Van Gorp et al., 2010; Patton et al., 2009

claim: Scavenger receptor cysteine-rich domain 5 (SRCR5) serves as the core domain for virus recognition in CD163.
source: Multiple studies have reported that CD163 is an essential receptor for PRRSV infection, with scavenger receptor cysteine-rich domain 5 (SRCR5) serving as the core domain for virus recognition (Calvert et al., 2007; Van Gorp et al., 2010; Patton et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calvert et al., 2007; Van Gorp et al., 2010; Patton et al., 2009

claim: Prather's group was the first to use CRISPR/Cas9 technology to generate SRCR5 domain-targeted CD163 knockout pigs in 2016.
source: In 2016, Prather's group was the first to use CRISPR/Cas9 technology to generate SRCR5 domain-targeted CD163 knockout pigs.
evidence: Stated as a historical fact in the manuscript

claim: A CD163 knockout line was completely resistant to genotype 2 PRRSV infection.
source: They demonstrated that a CD163 knockout line was completely resistant to genotype 2 PRRSV infection (Whitworth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitworth et al., 2016

claim: The CD163 SRCR5 domain was replaced with human CD163-Like SRCR8 domain to generate PRRSV genotype 1 resistance.
source: For example, the CD163 SRCR5 domain was replaced with human CD163-Like SRCR8 domain to generate PRRSV genotype 1 resistance (Wells et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wells et al., 2017

claim: Homozygous gene-edited Large White pigs with a 50 bp deletion in exon 7 of the CD163 gene are fully resistant to genotype 2 PRRSV.
source: Wei et al., 2018 reported homozygous gene-edited Large White pigs with a 50 bp deletion in exon 7 of the CD163 gene (Wei et al., 2018) that are fully resistant to genotype 2 PRRSV.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wei et al., 2018

claim: Deletion of the SRCR5 domain can generate resistance to both PRRSV genotypes.
source: There are also examples of deletion of the SRCR5 domain seeking resistance to both PRRSV genotypes (Burkard et al., 2017), or introducing a premature termination in the CD163 SRCR5 domain to generate HP-PRRSV (highly pathogenic PRRSV)-resistant Duroc pigs (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burkard et al., 2017

claim: Introducing a premature termination in the CD163 SRCR5 domain can generate HP-PRRSV (highly pathogenic PRRSV)-resistant Duroc pigs.
source: There are also examples of deletion of the SRCR5 domain seeking resistance to both PRRSV genotypes (Burkard et al., 2017), or introducing a premature termination in the CD163 SRCR5 domain to generate HP-PRRSV (highly pathogenic PRRSV)-resistant Duroc pigs (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018

claim: Deleting the SRCR5 LBP region generates PRRSV genotype 2 resistant pigs.
source: Deleting the SRCR5 LBP region has also been reported to generate a PRRSV genotype 2 resistant pigs (Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2019

claim: PRRSV-resistant pig breeds can be generated by editing the CD163 gene.
source: All these studies demonstrate that PRRSV-resistant pig breeds can be generated by editing the CD163 gene, enabling alleviation of the severity of PRRSV.
evidence: Inference drawn from multiple cited studies

claim: TGEV is an acute high-contact infectious virus that frequently co-infects with other porcine diarrhea-associated viruses such as PEDV and PoRV.
source: In addition to PRRSV, transmissible gastroenteritis virus (TGEV), an acute high-contact infectious virus, is known to frequently occur to co-infect with other porcine diarrhea-associated viruses such as porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV), porcine rotavirus (PoRV) (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013

claim: TGEV is globally distributed and causes tremendous economic losses in pork production.
source: TGEV is globally distributed and causes tremendous economic losses in pork production (Gerdts and Zakhartchouk, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gerdts and Zakhartchouk, 2017

claim: The mortality rate of TGEV-infected piglets under the age of 14 days approaches 100%.
source: Characterized by vomiting, severe diarrhea, and dehydration, the mortality rate of TGEV-infected piglets under the age of 14 days approaches 100%.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: TGEV is a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA coronavirus which targets pig intestinal epithelium for infection.
source: TGEV is a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA coronavirus which targets pig intestinal epithelium for infection (Brierley et al., 1989; Wesley and Lager, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brierley et al., 1989; Wesley and Lager, 2003

claim: The pAPN protein acts as a receptor in mediating TGEV infection.
source: Studies have shown that the pAPN protein acts as a receptor in mediating TGEV infection.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge from studies

claim: TGEV viral glycoproteins bind to pAPN receptors on the surface of small intestinal epithelial cells and mediate membrane fusion, resulting in the virus entering into epithelial cells.
source: The viral glycoproteins bind to pAPN receptors on the surface of small intestinal epithelial cells and mediate membrane fusion, thus resulting in the virus entering into epithelial cells (Delmas et al., 1992; Hansen et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delmas et al., 1992; Hansen et al., 1998

claim: Inhibition or direct knockout of pAPN in small intestinal epithelial cells can mitigate TGEV infection.
source: Inhibition or direct knockout of pAPN in small intestinal epithelial cells can mitigate TGEV infection (Ji et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ji et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018

claim: pAPN knockout pigs are resistant to TGEV.

evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 2019; Whitworth et al., 2019

claim: PDCoV is a highly virulent porcine coronavirus discovered in 2012 that causes watery diarrhea and vomiting in sows and piglets.
source: PDCoV is a highly virulent porcine coronavirus discovered in 2012 that causes watery diarrhea and vomiting in sows and piglets, with piglet mortality rates of 30% to 40% (Wang et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2012

claim: PDCoV has piglet mortality rates of 30% to 40%.

claim: There is controversy about whether or not pAPN is a functional receptor for PDCoV.

claim: pAPN functions as a receptor to promote PDCoV entry into cells.
source: Wang et al., 2018 showed that pAPN functions as a receptor to promote PDCoV entry into cells (Wang et al., 2018), while Zhu et al., 2018 confirmed its involvement but showed that pAPN was an unnecessary important functional receptor for PDCoV infection (Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: pAPN is an unnecessary important functional receptor for PDCoV infection.
source: Wang et al., 2018 showed that pAPN functions as a receptor to promote PDCoV entry into cells (Wang et al., 2018), while Zhu et al., 2018 confirmed its involvement but showed that pAPN was an unnecessary important functional receptor for PDCoV infection (Zhu et al., 2018).

source: It was suggested that pAPN may be one of the receptors for PDCoV, and an unknown receptor or factor may compensate for pAPN function in the absence of pAPN (Stoian et al., 2020).

source: Although gene-edited CD163 knockout (PRRV resistant) pigs and pAPN knockout (TGEV resistant) pigs have been previously generated, respectively, pigs that are resistant to the infection of both viruses are lacking.
